speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, September 16, consideration of Bill C-l 10, to amend the Export Development Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 3 and 5 (Mr. Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have the opportunity to address a few colleagues on amendments Nos. 3 and 5 to Bill C-l 10. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), deserves a great deal of credit for moving these amendments because by doing so he is drawing to the attention of Parliament a scandalous situation. Canadians are all too aware of the mounting deficits incurred by Crown corporations. Canadair, de Havilland, the Post Office, Consolidated Computer and VIA Rail have all made headlines recently as deficit-ridden corporations. As each corporation makes the headlines, the question arises as to how it could have happened. The blame is ultimately shifted to Parliament and it is to Parliament that Canadians look for redress. But, Mr. Speaker, no redress is found because Governments have given away Parliament's authority for reasons of political expediency.
[DOT]	(ii10)
Bill C-l 10 is designed to place the Export Development Corporation well beyond Parliament's reach. If the legislation passes without our amendments in place, then we have given the EDC an extremely long rope, and if it hangs itself on that rope Parliament will have very little to say about it.
The problem with the legislation is quite simple. It increases the authorized capital of the Export Development Corporation from $1 billion to $2 billion, which in turn increases the EDCs borrowing authority from $10 billion to $20 billion. Hence the EDC will be free to borrow as much as $20 billion before having to trouble itself with Parliament again. We cannot accept that, Mr. Speaker.
What is perhaps just as galling is the fact that there does not appear to be a particularly good reason for increasing the
authorized capital or the borrowing authority at this time. The Export Development Corporation's 1982 annual report set out existing authorized capital at $465 million and borrowing at less than $5 billion. Both figures are less than half existing limits. Why, we might well ask, do the limits need to be doubled? I believe it behooves the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) to provide the House with a full explanation for not accepting Motions Nos. 3 and 5.
In addition to this explanation, Mr. Speaker, the Minister should ask himself if the EDC will receive entirely the wrong message from that legislation. Despite the statistics, it remains a time of restraint. The federal Government cannot let the deficit rip in good time as well as in bad. There comes a time, and I suggest that time is near, that the Government must start trimming its sails as the private sector opens theirs.
The Export Development Corporation has not been a model of sleek efficiency. Last year 613 employees were on hand to cope with 62 exporters. Two of these exporters accounted for 50 per cent of the funds. That is almost ten employees for each customer, Mr. Speaker. In addition to the 62 customers, the EDC employees wrote up approximately 900 export insurance policies or about one and a half policies per employee over a one-year period. I am not launching an attack on the EDC, Mr. Speaker. I am simply pointing out that additional borrowing authority is neither necessary nor advisable. If the signal from the Government to the EDC is one of: "Here is an extra $10 billion on top of the $5 billion you have yet to use", then where is the incentive to run a lean operation? The EDC would have more credit than it could use and neither the EDC nor the Government would need worry about Parliament for a long, long time.
We have seen that the track record of too many Crown corporations has not been good. These corporations have escaped public scrutiny precisely because of legislation like Bill C-l 10. We on this side are of the opinion that the public has had quite enough of this and wants to see Parliament reassert control. No control is possible if the Government continues to use its numbers to ram through legislation which sidesteps Parliament. The Auditor General has already referred to Crown corporations as a subgovernment.
Part of what the Auditor General is getting at is the new relationship which is becoming too much the rule, the new relationship between the Government and Crown corporations. Parliament is excluded from that relationship because Parliament has been legislated out of an active place in the Crown corporation's existence. The time to halt this slide into irrelevance is now, and one positive step would be to adopt Motions Nos. 3 and 5.

Before concluding, however, 1 believe it is worth our while to see how the Export Development Corporation's United States counterpart has operated. After all, the Minister of State for International Trade has recently concluded that our trade interest lies chiefly with the United States. The Minister might then wish to go a step further and see how the Americans operate. 1 wonder, as an aside, if one of the high school classes in my riding of Northumberland could have reached the same conclusion about Canada's trade policy at a great deal less cost to the taxpayer.
The Export-Import Bank of the United States is a rough counterpart to the Export Development Corporation. That bank has paid-in capital of $1 billion and borrowings of $16 billion. What is proposed in Bill C-l 10 is authorized capital of $2 billion, twice the amount of the United States counterpart, and borrowing authority of $20 billion, a great deal more than the Export-Import Bank. Who is the Government trying to kid? Our population is one-tenth that of the United States, and our trade volume is considerably less, yet the Americans are operating at less potential cost than is proposed in Bill C-l 10.
1 suggest that it is time to put Canada's tax base into perspective. The taxpayers of Northumberland naturally want to see Canada's trade expanded, and we all do, but not at any cost. If the Government's intention with Bill C-l 10 is to increase the dollars available to subsidize loans to foreign purchasers, then I am even more adamantly opposed. It is not much of a sale if the selling price is less than the cost. Surely to goodness, it makes far more sense to use the taxpayer's dollars to assist Canadian enterprises which can or could make bona fide overseas sales. Monuments in Algeria do not help the unemployed in the county of Northumberland.
The Canadian people have made it abundantly clear that they want Parliament to tighten its control over runaway expenditures. People are sick to death of scrounging for rent and mortgage payments while reading about billion dollar deficits. Accountability is a must, and Bill C-l 10 cripples that. We on this side do not expect to be able to stop the legislation, but there can be little reason for the Government not to adopt Motions Nos. 3 and 5. I strongly urge it to do so.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to rise this morning to speak to Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Corporation. I am also pleased to see the Minister here since it is relatively unusual to see Ministers in the House day after day listening to comments for or against their Bills.
The amendments presented by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) are in Motions Nos. 3 and 5. Motion 3 proposes to reduce the authorized capital from two billion, one hundred dollars to one billion, one hundred dollars. Motion 5 is to limit the borrowings so that they do not exceed ten times the paid-in capital and surplus of the company.
If we look at some of the statistics related to the Export Development Corporation, we see that it now has an authorized capital of one billion, one hundred dollars. It has a paid-in capital and surplus of $651 million and its earnings in 1982 were approximately $1 million. In order to earn that $1 million it placed $2.46 billion in loans in 1982 through 63 transactions. There were 613 employees to carry out these 63 transactions. In other words, there were ten employees for each transaction.
When we study this information further we find that for the $651 million which the Government has invested in this corporation it only earned $1 million in 1982, which represents one-quarter of 1 per cent return on capital. What Canadian could operate a business with a .25 per cent return on capital? In effect, this means that it is an inefficient corporation. There are no checks and balances in this corporation, which I will expand upon in a few minutes when I talk about the paid-in capital versus authorized capital.
There is no efficiency lodged with EDC because of this provision. Since there is no efficiency built into the corporation, it does not have to obtain a reasonable rate of return on its capital. Yet the citizens of this country are subsidizing this corporation when it receives a return of .25 per cent on its capital.
I believe the Minister said that no industrialized country in the world is more dependent on exports than Canada. While I admit that we are dependent on exports, 1 suggest that his statement is not true. Technically speaking, Japan is more dependent on exports than Canada. Certainly we are dependent and need exports, but to say that no industrialized country is more dependent than us is an overstatement at least.
Where is the need for this increased lending? EDC has not demonstrated that it needs to increase its authorized capital. It is not using all that it has at the moment even though we disagree with some of the provisions. When a private sector corporation seeks to increase its authorized capital, it usually demonstrates the need. This is not so with Government organizations such as this. In effect, the Government wishes to remove this control of borrowing authority from Parliament and lodge it with the bureaucracy which is then not accountable to Parliament.
If we look at some of the corporations that the Government has set up, we can see some very peculiar things. One can think of Petro-Canada and what a great corporation it is for Canadians. Its potential loss this year will be approximately $15 million. It has laid off 25 per cent of its staff over the last year. It recently negotiated the leasing of 240,000 square feet in a building which it leased in Calgary last year at $21 a square foot. The building has been empty since that time and Petro-Canada is offering to sublease the building at zero rent; one only has to pay the operating costs for the space. That is the "efficiency" built into the bureaucracy by this Government.

We do not have to look much further than Canadair which lost SI.4 billion last year. If that is not bad enough, the new corporation which the Government intends to set up to oversee these corporations, the Canada Development Investment Corporation, will take on all of the debts of Canadair amounting to $1.35 billion. The Canadian people have to pay that sum. We now have to assume Canadair's debts. This is an example of efficiency in Crown corporations.
We can talk about de Havilland which lost approximately $364 million in 1982 and will have a substantial loss again this year, as will Canadair. We can talk about CIDA. CIDA provides loans to other countries. At the end of the Government's fiscal year, it is not unusual for the Government to give countries which apply for loans more money than they ask for. This is done because the agency wants the money spent before year end, otherwise its allotment could be cut back. This is the "efficiency" built into these Crown corporations. There are no checks and balances. There is no control. We in this Party are trying to restore that control. We do not think the additional capital is needed.
The Government wants borrowing authority ten times the authorized capital. Motion No. 5 by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South seeks to restrict that borrowing to ten times the paid-in capital. That will put a balance and check into the corporation so that efficiency would become the norm rather than the exception. The corporation will have to attempt to increase its earnings. This will allow it to loan out more money based on its built-in surplus. At the moment there is no indication that the corporation has to earn any money.
We are not opposed to the principle of the Bill, but we are opposed to some of the provisions. The amendments moved by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South are worth-while motions.
I would like to conclude by reading a couple of points from the Auditor General's Report. Since 1976 various Auditors General have been indicating their concern about the lack of accountability of Government organizations. The first quotation is this:
In the majority of Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually nonexistent.
This, together with the results of a prior year's study of similar practices in departments, led the Auditor General to express the deep concern that Parliament-indeed, the Government-had lost, or was close to losing, effective control of the public purse.
The Auditor General's report goes on:
Parliament's involvment both in establishing and overseeing Crown-owned corporations is essential for effective accountability.
At the present time Crown corporations are not accountable to Parliament. Only Members of Parliament are. Unless we bring back that control, we will lose complete control over Government spending.
Export Development Act

Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the Export Development Act for a few moments and to refer specifically to the Export Development Corporation, which provides yet another example of a branch of Government that is out of control and no longer accountable to Parliament. The fact of the matter is that the Export Development Corporation is rapidly on its way to becoming a bureaucratic nightmare. It has a history of making unsound loans to foreign countries, borrowing and lending money at ever increasing rates, extending its empire, and involving Canada in deals which are both expensive and can be proven very inefficient. For instance, the corporation quite often does business for the Government of Canada and, under the provisions of the EDC, can authorize up to $2.5 billion just by Order in Council, a decision of Cabinet, a decision that never comes before the elected representatives of the country. As of December 31, 1982, the Government spent $753 million of taxpayers' money in this manner-Orders in Council.
But this is only the beginning of an horrendous nightmare. There are some 613 employees of the corporation. They have offices in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal and Halifax, with their head office in Ottawa. This translates into almost ten employees for each separate loan customer. This is a fine example of Government mismanagement and economic inefficiency. What bank, what trust company or what lending institution could exist on a ratio like that? It is little wonder that we are burdened with the billion dollar deficit figures which continue to restrict and impede our economic recovery.
For instance, after investing $691 million of public capital, the corporation was able to show a profit of only slightly more than $1 million. This type of gross ineffectiveness is unacceptable to this Party and I am sure to the people of Canada. To make matters worse, we Parliamentarians have literally no control whatsoever over the workings of the corporation.
It is the serious question of accountability which 1 would now like to address by analysing a number of inequities that arise out of the Export Development Act. To begin with, I would like to discuss Section 11(2) of the Act which reads:
Where the board recommends that the Minister subscribe for unissued shares of the corporation, the Minister may, if the Minster of Finance concurs, subscribe for such shares at par as he considers desirable and there shall be paid to the corporation the amount of each subscription out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund at such times and in such amounts as the board requires.
In other words, this authorizes the Government to treat the matter as statutory, as law, effectively eliminating the possibility of a parliamentary vote. We have seen examples of that in the not too distant past. As usual it means that taxpayers are denied the basic rights of a democratic society, and their hard-earned dollars are displaced at the whim of yet another bureaucratic monster.
Also I would like to draw attention to Section 31 of the Act which reads:
(1) Where the Minister reports to the Governor in Council that (a) the board is of the opinion that a proposed loan or guarantee of the kind described in Section 29 would, if made or issued, before a term or in an amount

Export Development Act
in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one export transaction, person, country, government or agency thereof or in relation to a particular export transaction, person, country, government or agency thereof, and
(b) in the opinion of the Minister it is in the national interest that the proposed loan be made or guarantee issued, the Governor in Council may authorize the corporation to make the proposed loan or give the proposed guarantee, as the case may be.
In effect, loans of this nature may be made by the corporation, by the convenient method of Order in Council. Once again parliamentary authority has been drastically superseded and the current Government has managed to go one step further in eroding the magnanimous institution known as Government.
While continuing its assault on parliamentary tradition, the Government simultaneously manages to interfere at an alarming rate in the business of the private sector. This is very disturbing to our Party. It is by now quite evident that a great deal of the activities currently delegated to the Export Development Corporation could successfully be turned over to private enterprise with the proper reorientation and structuring, where the dollars would be spent with far more justification than, as referred to earlier today, in monuments built in Algeria. Also the funding has been conducted on a narrow basis with a great deal going to limited sources.
In conclusion, the Progressive Conservative Party looks upon the Export Development Corporation, as it does all other Crown corporations, with a great deal of scrutiny and concern for control of the public purse. There is a serious need for increased control by Government and increased accountability to Parliament as recommended by the reports of the Lambert Commission, the Auditor General and the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. I am afraid from time to time that these reports go unnoticed by the Government.
The present structure of the corporation being discussed today is not conducive to efficiency and cost accountability. Funds must not be allowed to be granted solely by Order in Council or a decision of Cabinet behind closed doors without proper parliamentary debate. For this and many other reasons, the arrangement currently prevailing must be eradicated by amendments in favour of a structure more accountable to Canadian taxpayers.
We have had enough of monuments being built at taxpayers' expense. We have had enough of Crown corporations spending at will the dollars of Canadian taxpayers without a word being said in this place about where such decisions should be made. I am sure Hon. Members on the Government side as well as those on the Opposition side would like to know more than Cabinet knows about decisions concerning the spending of taxpayers' dollars. We hope there will be sufficient amendments to the Act we are discussing today to return accountability to where it should be, here in Parliament with its elected Members, whose sole job it is to represent the constituents who sent them here to speak on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on behalf of my Party to the amendments now before the House. The entire question of the Export Development Act
and the institutions for which it provides are very important to the country. Anything concerning the relations of a modern state such as Canada with other countries and states is important. Naturally I am interested in different parts of our relationships with other countries. The export development part is extremely important. Another area of particular interest is the matter of international aid. Both these areas are closely linked.
I have difficulty accepting some of the facts which the Progressive Conservatives bring forward about the misuse of aid. The example which has been given repeatedly of a monument in Algeria-unfortunately I have never seen it-is a poor example of Canadian aid; but I know of hundreds of examples where aid has truly helped and brought about better lives for many people. I would say that a broader look in this regard is required.
In so far as these amendments are concerned, I think we are at a small logjam. Yesterday I travelled through a portion of Quebec and saw some logs. As soon as I saw them I remembered the stories about logjams. In a logjam, the logs pile up because certain logs will not break loose. If someone finds the logs causing the problem and dynamites them or uses some other means, the logs begin to move again. With regard to this Bill, if the Minister was willing to discuss some concessions with the Opposition, we might be able to get out of our present logjam and get this Bill moving again.
There are basically two problems with the amendments now under discussion. The first is that the Government is asking for $2 billion in this Bill and the Opposition is speaking to $1 billion. As others have mentioned, $2 billion is a large amount. I wonder whether there is a possibility of the two sides coming to an agreement and rather than $1 billion or $2 billion, there could be a meeting of the ways somewhere in between. It is necessary to reach a compromise in order to get the Bill moving. Possibly we could speak about $1.5 billion and agree to such an amendment.
I suggest that the Minister and the Opposition think in those terms. Possibly we could find a middle of the road solution which recognizes the Opposition speaking against the $2 billion in funding, but at the same time satisfying the Government.
There is a second matter holding up the passage of this Bill. Here, too, a compromise could be reached. The Opposition is asking that the majority of the directors be from the private sector. I can see that as something the Minister could accept. Everybody who would be a director would be a Canadian. I cannot see that the ministry would suffer if people were selected from both the public and private sectors, with the majority from the private sector. I do not see any difficulty with that. If we want brains, skills, history and experience, the Minister should be conscious of the fact that that kind of Opposition move is an interesting point of view. I do not think the Bill or Canada's relationship with other parts of the world would suffer.
September 19, 1983

I ask the Minister to look seriously at the two problems I have mentioned and to work with the Opposition in finding a solution in order that we can clear up the logjam and get the Bill under way. What is important is that we live in a very mobile, rapid society. International society is moving at a great speed. Anything that stops Canadian input into the world society causes a problem. It is a problem that we face and one which affects every Canadian.
This Bill could be moved along with compromise between the Opposition and the Government. All of us want to see an Export Development Act put in place, one that will bring about international relationships between Canada as a modern nation state and other modern nation states.
This is a complicated world and this is a very complicated situation. Even if we bring in more people from the private sector as directors, 1 do not think that will be an absolute solution. I do not see that in our modern times. If the brains, skills and goodwill are there, the Minister should consider appointing the majority of directors from that area of the country. We will not lose anything in the long run.
The Minister should also consider the fact that the Opposition is opposed to the $2 billion figure. It is just too much. At the same time, the Government is considering cutting back on our aid program. I suggest if we could cut back with this Bill, some of those funds could be used for aid programs. If the Minister and the Opposition could discuss these points, I feel that the Bill could move forward. That would be for the good of us all. It would be the right thing to do.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-110. The tragedy of Canada is that the federal Government continually demonstrates that it has no feel for the mood of the country and has no apparent desire to understand the psychology of its people. This is the product of a Government that is stale, having been too long in office. For more than a decade the only thing important to this Government was to appeal to central Canada's electoral majority, ignoring in the process any necessity to relate to the yearnings of the people generally.
Ignoring people has become the mark of this Government. We have seen this in a number of issues of the day, such as metrication and in the objectionable, insensitive manner in which it has pursued the legitimate goals which pertain to Canada's two languages, as well as in the national energy policy. We have seen this in the Government's mammoth appetite for spending which has produced deficits so large as to be unimaginable just a few years ago. We have also seen it in Government interference and the injection of regulations into nearly every aspect of the life of the individual and the business community. Unfortunately, we have seen it in the divisive nature of its dealings with the Provinces and other areas.
Now, when the people of Canada are crying out for governments to truly show restraint by paring their expenditures and demands on the Treasury, the national Government of Canada persists in maintaining its extravagances and its waste based
Export Development Act
on a detailed commitment to control the economy and the nation.
The single act of restraint by this Government was the enactment of the six and five legislation. Having done so little in the direction of reducing its commitment to spending the nation into poverty, this Liberal Government now shows through every piece of legislation which it puts before the House and the nation that its real intent is to expand its influence and its control over Canadians in every aspect of their lives. This is at a time when people throughout the world are begging governments to back off. In Canada we saw this desire of the people demonstrated in Saskatchewan, which rid itself of a burdensome socialist Government. The people of British Columbia made that same point in re-electing the Government headed by Premier Bill Bennett. For those who may not show much interest in what happens outside of central Canada, I might point out that the main issue in that election was the question of Government spending. If elected, the NDP proposed to provide more programs, fewer constraints and to spend more, which has been the tradition of that Party wherever it has achieved power. The people of British Columbia soundly rejected the NDP platform, supporting Mr. Bennett's call for a leaner, more efficient Government service, more accountable to the people.
The necessity of greater accountability was identified last fall by Canada's Auditor General, who said:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of Government activities. The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of Government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds.
It is because of this focus of accountability that we are being most critical of Bill C-110. It is within the areas of restraint and accountability that the Government has been most irresponsible in carrying out its mandate.
Bill C-l 10 is another example of this. Let us look at what it attempts to achieve. It would alter the current structure of the board of directors, thus increasing its power. It would increase the number of directors that the Government can appoint to 15 from 12 to reflect Government priorities. It would give full authority to the Export Development Corporation to take property as security. It would double the authorized capital to $2 billion of taxpayers' money. It would permit the corporation to borrow up to $20 billion for any of its purposes. It would permit the corporation to accept insurance liabilities up to a further $20 billion. It would expand the definition of the types of transactions in which the Export Development Corporation may involve itself. It would give authority to the corporation to subsequently alter an agreement or guarantee which had been undertaken on the direction of the Governor in Council.
It is interesting to observe that any loss, expense or default which may ensue would be chargeable to the taxpayer through the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Elsewhere in the Act there is a built-in authority for the Cabinet to intrude and force upon
