Export Development Act
the corporation actions which may not be in its interests or in the interests of Canada as a whole. All of this is done outside the purview of Parliament.
Bill C-l 10 will increase from $2.5 billion to $10 billion the amount of liability which the Cabinet can impose upon the corporation by Order in Council, and always without going to Parliament for approval. In this, as in so much of its legislation, the Government bypasses Parliament with a blank cheque provision. According to Professor Andre Raynault of the University of Montreal, the Export Development Corporation is "rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient."
The amendments to the Bill that we have put forward are designed to restore the degree of accountability to Parliament which is a necessary ingredient of parliamentary democracy. We would leave the authorized capital at $1 billion and, most important, to bring rational economic considerations into play, we would restrict the corporation's borrowings to ten times the actual paid-up capital, plus any earned surplus.
Our friend to the left said that he did not appreciate the references to the Algerian monument to Marxism. I believe this incident requires repeated emphasis because it demonstrates the length to which the Export Development Corporation can go if it is allowed a free hand, given too much money and the licence to spend money to create its own priorities. We are not impressed by such deals as the Algerian monument to Marxism. The Export Development Corporation lent that country nearly $100 million at 7 per cent interest at a time when Canadians were paying 20 per cent or more. Restricting the amount of the borrowing authority of the corporation would certainly serve to curb this type of excess which so offends Canadians.
Financing of the Export Development is obtained by the corporation borrowing on the credit of Canada on the international money markets so as to finance the sale of Canadian goods. With the Government guarantee, the corporation is able to borrow money on the international market at a cheaper rate than any commercial borrower. The farmers of Canada would ask the Government why the Farm Credit Corporation, which is so restricted in capital that it is no longer making loans in some areas, has not been given the authority to borrow on the capital markets of the world at a favourable rate so that it can service Canadian farmers to a greater degree.
It is the purpose and responsibility of the elected Parliamentarians of Canada to exercise control over the purse strings of the national treasury. I find it difficult to understand the reluctance of Hon. Members opposite to accept that democratic principle.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak in this debate concerning Bill C-l 10, to amend the Export Development Act, and the motions moved by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I find myself in my place in the House of Commons debating a piece of Government legislation which seeks to circumvent the prime responsibility of Parliament. Once again, I find myself in opposition to another Liberal attempt to deny Parliament its historical right as guardian of the taxpayers' funds.
What I find particularly obnoxious is that the federal Government can produce funds like pulling rabbits out of a hat for the Export Development Corporation for activities the public is not even aware of, while on the other hand it has difficulty providing funds to the Farm Credit Corporation for Canadian farmers who are in real need.
At first glance one would believe that Bill C-l 10, a Bill to amend the Export Development Act, and particularly Motions Nos. 3 and 5, are truly comparable to the motherhood issue. After all, who could speak against the export of capital goods from Canada and therefore the creation of much needed jobs? But we must also realize that there is something far greater at stake here, and that is the role of parliamentary authority and control of the public purse.
Fiscal responsibility and the lack of accountability to Parliament is the real question raised in this Bill. The Bill allows the Export Development Corporation's board of directors to spend $60 billion dollars without accounting to Parliament until after it is spent. The people of Canada are beginning to ask questions about how the Government has spent and is spending their money. Because Crown corporation after Crown corporation has lost the confidence of the Canadian public, people want parliamentary control of public funds. It is not unreasonable to expect that appropriations should come before the House as they are required, but not with this blank cheque approach. The House of Commons has lost control over Crown corporations, to say the least. We do not even know how many there are, let alone how much money is involved or for what valid reasons they are doing business. No one is questioning the validity of the EDC. What is being questioned is the authority of Parliament and our ability to question the spending of public funds before, not after, they are spent.
It is difficult to imagine what $60 billion really is, but I am told that just $1 million in $1 bills laid end to end would stretch from this Chamber to Sharbot Lake, a community in my riding 80 miles away. Just imagine how far $60 billion in $1 bills would go.
We are now considering $20 billion of borrowing authority to be lent to various concerns around the world. The Farm Credit Corporation needs another $300 million but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) say no. The amendment we are dealing with today reduces the capital to $1 billion, $100 instead of authorized capital of $2 billion.
We hear a great deal of flak from Government Members about what a PC Government would do. Mr. Speaker, this Party has for some time, including 1979 when we were the Government for a short period, promoted parliamentary reform. Parliamentary procedures must be put in place that scrutinize expenditures before they are spent rather than after.
September 19, 1983

I urge the Minister responsible to consider these amendments to this Act and to start the process of giving some accountability back to Members of Parliament and, therefore, to the people of Canada. Year after year the Auditor General warns that financial management and control of departments and agencies is well below acceptable standards. The raising and spending of money goes to the very heart of the role Parliament plays. My colleagues and 1 are determined that this institution shall retain the integrity and responsibility with which it was originally endowed.
Recently 1 read in the local press that over 50 per cent of the Canadian population believes that the role of Parliament in our society is limited. With the current situation which the federal Government is trying to develop, I see this situation deteriorating, not improving. Fiscal accountability is fundamental to the rights of Parliament. Unless that responsibility is strengthened and preserved, I am afraid the institution we know as Parliament will cease to exist.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, has pointed out, among other things, the lack of private sector businessmen to sit on the reconstituted board of directors of the Export Development Corporation. Our desire to place businessmen on the board of directors of the EDC is to inspire a sense of reality in the decisions of the Crown corporation. As has been stated on several occasions in this House, the monument to the Algerian revolution which was financed by Canadian taxpayers is an example of where the isolated world of the civil servant lacks credibility.
In the same vein, I shake my head in disbelief when I witness this Government's response to the agricultural community. My Party has advocated on numerous occasions policies which would help farmers who are currently caught in the web of high interest rates, policies which would provide long-term credit at affordable interest rates. However, the Minister of Finance does not believe that farm bankruptcies are occurring, and he does not believe that the current situation in which a farmer finds himself when he approaches major lending institutions is cause for concern. It was reputed earlier this year that a mid-eastern country offered Canada money at 7 per cent interest to be repaid with food supplies, and the Government refused. The Minister of Finance is said to have stated that we did not need it.
The Government now wishes to develop a new wrinkle in deficit financing for its Crown corporations. Currently, a trust company or other financial institution must have money in the till to do business. They are able to borrow in ratio to their paid-in capital and earned surplus. This Act will allow the Export Development Corporation to borrow ten times its authorized capital. In layman's terms there may be only one dollar in the till, but the company is authorized to borrow $10 billion even if it has nothing with which to back this borrowing. The federal Government will allow this to occur. This represents no control whatsoever and is totally irresponsible.
The federal Government can find money to build monuments to a revolution in Algeria, but when the federal Govern-
Export Development Act
ment is requested to provide the necessary funds to help the average Canadian farmer produce food and hold off bankruptcy, a condition which has not developed through any action on the part of the farmer but through the high interest policy of the Government, the federal Government states that current funding is adequate.
Past experience dictates that parliamentary control of spending is necessary. Out of the 62 companies which received EDC financing last year, three companies received more than half the total. EDC has no business financing foreign development which will jeopardize jobs in this country. However, it would be remiss of me to claim that a double standard exists because I do not believe this Government operates by any standard of conduct. This Government could regain some stature if it would allow Parliament its natural historical prerogative of accountability for the taxpayers' dollars.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will have heard in the last few days a number of speakers rise in their places in this House and address themselves to Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Corporation. The reason. Sir, that a number of Hon. Members have been rising to speak is in the dim, fleeting hope that somehow or other the Government might get the message that there are major things wrong with the Bill which it is presenting to the House. We hope, like advertising with its repetition, that with the repetition of that message to the Government it will finally sink in. I have been watching the response of Government Members this morning and I must say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I really do not see the dawning of any recognition on their faces as yet. I can hope and 1 can pray, and I trust that they will come to that recognition before this debate is over.
The amendments which have been put forward by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) are really worth while considering. There is no question but that they would improve this Bill. Beyond the amendments which the Hon. Member has put to the House, there are ramifications in this Bill which extend well beyond Canadian trade policy, well beyond the Export Development Act itself, well beyond Crown corporations, and which come to the fundamental reason why this House exists and what parliamentary tradition is all about. It goes to the very heart of our system of government.
1 would like to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, right at the outset, that we all understand, appreciate and value the position of trade policy in our over-all operations, in our economy. We know how important it is. We think there should be greater emphasis by the Government on creating the proper economic climate, the proper environment in this country for an expansion of Canadian trade policy. Not that it will be limited, not that it will be restricted, but that it will be expanded. That will mean a stronger economy. It will mean more jobs. It will mean greater prosperity in this country. It is necessary, indeed, that Government provide that climate as much as possible. It is, therefore, not a question of trade policy which is under scrutiny or attack here. It is the provisions by which the Government is trying to bring about the extension or

September 19, 1983
Export Development Act
the amendment of the mandate of the Export Development Corporation.
As we have seen, the Government intends to double the authorized capital of the Export Development Corporation. This means that the corporation will then be able to borrow up to $20 billion as opposed to the original $10 billion which it had been authorized to borrow. The Government may also now make insurance commitments by Order in Council which are not of a proper commercial nature. It will be able to make these commitments up to a ceiling of $10 billion instead of the original $3.5 billion. This will all be done without any parliamentary approval.
That is what 1 meant when I said that this Bill goes much beyond trade policy or the Export Development Corporation or Crown corporations. It is the fact that the Government is trying to do this without proper parliamentary approval, which I oppose most strongly and which my Party opposes most strongly. It is in an effort to redress this situation that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, has put forward his proposals.
As elected officials representing Canadians from coast to coast, we as Hon. Members of this House have a responsibility to see that the public purse is scrutinized at all times. That is where Parliament began. That is the foundation upon which it was laid. And, Sir, not only are parliamentary expenditures to be scrutinized, but it is to be shown to the people of Canada that those expenditures are not being abused. Because, after all, it is not our money or the Government of Canada's money; it is the hard earned income of millions of Canadians which is being discussed here.
There will be people, Mr. Speaker, who would like to ask whether the borrowers who are able to take advantage of the borrowing measures under the EDC are going to get more preferential rates than, say, the small business community in Canada. More importantly, will the small business community of Canada ever know what those preferential rates might be? So much of this is done in secrecy, Sir, without the scrutiny of Parliament. If one were to look, as has been mentioned here many times, at some of the readily available examples of spending which have not been approved by this House or even come before this House, then one can see the potential for abuse which lies in the Bill as presented to us. It becomes very clearly visible. Some of these examples have been mentioned on a number of occasions and I wish the Government would take them to heart.
The fact is that Canadair lost $1.4 billion and that was never allowed to be scrutinized by Parliament, de Havilland lost $226 million, Via Rail lost $440 million, and Canada Post lost $300 million. There was no scrutiny by the elected Members of Parliament of those Crown agencies which together lost a total of over $2 billion. No one here in this House of Commons or in a parliamentary committee had a chance to examine that situation, and these are just four of more than 300 Crown corporations presently in existence.
Sir, 1 would like to refer to a statement made in the Report of the Lambert Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability some four years ago. The Report warned the Government of what would happen if the essence of accountability was further eroded. Commissioner Lambert said this:
In examining the bewildering array of Crown agencies we have found that existing provisions for classifying them and for accountability for each category have been rendered obsolete. The resulting state of confusion, if left unattended, will seriously impair the value of these agencies as instruments of public purpose and do further damage to the tenuous and sometimes obscure accountability links that... they now have with the Government and Parliament.
He talked about the obscure accountability links and said they were in danger of being further eroded. Despite this warning the Government is now seeking to increase the funding available to another Crown corporation which is not adequately accountable to Parliament, and more importantly not accountable to the Canadian taxpayer; and we on this side find this simply unacceptable.
The importance of having Crown corporations strictly accountable to Parliament, Mr. Speaker, was emphasized once again in the Auditor General's Report last fall, which said this:
The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of Government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for over-seeing receipts and expenditures of public funds.
I see you are rising in your place, Mr. Speaker. In closing, I just want to reiterate that what the Auditor General was talking about was the fundamental responsibility of Parliament to be accountable for the expenditure of funds. 1 remind you, Sir, and through you the Government, that King Charles I lost his head because he refused to acknowledge the supremacy of Parliament. I predict, Mr. Speaker, this Government will lose not only its head but its position to your right, Sir, because it continues to ignore the supremacy of Parliament.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my friends on the Government side and to my left in the New Democratic Party may find this almost impossible to believe, but 1 had no intention of speaking on Bill C-110, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, including the amendments put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Coming as I do from the world of broadcast journalism, I never exported anything except perhaps ideas. I have never even had relatives who were remotely connected with the Export Development Corporation, at least that I know of. So I have not had the benefit of learning the intricacies of the exporting business, nor do I serve on the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. So Hon. Members can see from my credentials that I enter this debate with a pristine pure mind, without prejudice, without biases cluttered up by technicalitities.
1 must say that I do believe in the principle of an Export Development Corporation in terms of its benefits to the
September 19, 1983

Canadian economy, and the Government must create a climate to expand our trading opportunities.
What has brought me to my feet today, Mr. Speaker, is a weekend's reflection on the many excellent points made by my colleagues in their interventions on Bill C-110 during last week's deliberations on the subject. Members from one end of this country to the other, from the Western Arctic to Erie in my part of southern Ontario, all sounded alarmed about the implications of this legislation if this House passes what the Government wants in connection with the EDC. The two buzz phrases which caught my attention over and over again were "Crown corporation bureaucrats" and "no control by Parliament".
Well, Mr. Speaker, I may not be an expert in high finance but I do know something about the danger to our democratic way of life, particularly the damage to our rising defict, when Crown corporations run by bureaucrats run amok. As one who has watched and reported and loved Parliament for 25 years, I know of, and indeed fear, the prospect that we as elected representatives may have literally no control over the actions of this Export Development Corporation. Even if the average citizen on the street has not the slightest idea of what the EDC is or does, that person understands one thing very clearly: a Government money grab. I wonder how the man or woman on the street would react to the prospect of this Liberal Government allowing the EDC to make loans in the billions of dollars without myself or any other Member of Parliament needing to approve them. That is something that every Canadian citizen can and should know.
What we have before us in Bill C-l 10 is a bureaucratically controlled mechanism, which means that the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), the Hon. Member for Huron-Bruce (Mr. Cardiff), the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald), the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid), the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) and any of the other Hon. Members here would not be able to vote upon this and we would be regarded as totally unnecessary. Well, I am sorry, Mr. Minister, but my constituents in Hamilton-Wentworth just will not buy that complete lack of a parliamentary safeguard. Otherwise, why are we here if the House of Commons cannot question and control the Government's spending powers?
Bill C-l 10 touches the very heart of Parliament. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), put simply and eloquently why we on this side are so concerned about the accountability and control of the public purse when he said:
Our country has a parliamentary system under which the Government should be reflecting the thinking of the people. 1 want to tell the Hon. Members of the Government that this section does not reflect the thinking of Canadians. The polls have shown that Canadians are heartsore over what has been happening.
Export Development Act
The present Government is no longer representing what the people want. It has been telling the people what is good for them for a number of years and this Bill is a typical example of where the Government has given authority to a group of appointed people to spend money that has not been authorized by the House of Commons or the Senate. That is basically wrong.
The section to which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River was referring, is the one that we are trying to correct. Just to refresh the memories of Hon. Members and to point out the importance of the amendments before us, let me read Motions Nos. 3 and 5. Motion No. 3 states:
That Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended in Clause 5 by striking out lines 23 to 26 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"11.(1) The authorized capital of the Corporation is one billion one hundred dollars divided into ten million and one shares with a par value of one hundred dollars each."
Motion No. 5 states:
That Bill C-l 10, An Act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended in Clause 7 by striking out lines 39 to 41 at page 3 and lines 1 and 2 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"14. The aggregate amount of borrowings of the Corporation pursuant to sections 12 and 13 shall not exceed the amount equal to ten times the aggregate of the paid in capital and earned surplus in the accounts of the Corporation."
The explanation, as I see it, may be stated quite simply: the Government proposes that there be $2 billion in authorized capital for the corporation and that the aggregate amount of borrowing of the corporation shall "not exceed an amount equal to ten times the authorized capital of the corporation". Therefore, if one puts the Government's proposal against our amendments, one finds that the Government proposes to allow the corporation to borrow $20 billion without further parliamentary authorization. That is the basis for our strong objections, the objections taken by many Hon. Members in the debate.
Several Hon. Members have pointed out that it has become almost routine when dealing with the Government to speak in terms of "a billion dollars" or "a half-billion dollars" or "hundreds of millions of dollars", figures which are almost impossible for the average person to comprehend; yet here in this Bill the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) is attempting a money grab of gigantic proportions.
The provision with which we are now dealing calls for a total capitalization of the Export Development Corporation of $2 billion. When one multiplies that by ten-and that is the way the Bill works-one is considering that the Government is asking for $20 billion of lending authority which, in turn, means borrowing authority. That money comes from the taxpayers of this country. The Liberal Government proposes to accomplish this without parliamentary accountability because the Export Development Corporation does not have its spending scrutinized by Parliament. It is not required to table an operating budget, a capital budget or even to provide information on the size of its payroll. The mind boggles.
Earlier 1 mentioned the proliferation of Crown corporations in this country and how their spending can run amok. Let me conclude these brief remarks by quoting Professor Andre Raynauld, who is president-elect of the Economic Association

September 19, 1983
Export Development Act
of Canada, former President of the Economic Council of Canada, and a former Liberal M.N.A. in Quebec. This is what Professor Raynauld says about the Export Development Corporation:
It is rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient.
A poll taken during the summer indicated that a large number of Canadians consider Parliament to be irrelevant. People do not feel that Parliamentarians are representing them or protecting their interests. That is what we on this side are determined to do in connection with Bill C-110. Through our amendments we are determined to make the Export Development Corporation accountable to the people. That is why I, as well as many other Members of Parliament concerned about control over the public purse, decided to enter the debate today. I thank the House for its attention.
Mir. Stan Darling (Parry Sound-Muskoka): Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in the debate on Bill C-110. 1 am delighted to have the opportunity to speak on Motions Nos. 3 and 5, the amendments which were put forth by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). The amendments to the Bill call for an increase in the capitalization of the Export Development Corporation. Of course, we wish the amount to be reduced from $2 billion as requested in the Bill.
When it comes to Crown agencies and the experience we have had in the House over the past number of years, our main focus of attention should be accountability and control of the expenditure of taxpayers' money.
The amendments brought forth have been introduced for the purpose of closer scrutiny by elected Parliamentarians to correct the inadequacies of accountability that are present in the Bill as it stands. The increase of capital authority to the Export Development Corporation from $1 billion to $2 billion should be further reviewed. This would give the Export Development Corporation the authority to borrow up to ten times against the capital authority. Is this really warranted? This means $20 billion worth of borrowing authority. In total, the Bill will increase to $62 billion the amount of money that the Export Development Corporation can borrow, lend and insure, all without adequate parliamentary scrutiny and control. The Government is asking for a blank cheque, and the answer should be no.
Although there may be good reasons for this extra borrowing authority, the purse strings do have to be tightened. As the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) stated in the House earlier in the debate, the Export Development Corporation is not the only organization that finances exports; the vast majority of this financing is done by the private banking system, as it should be. We must see to it that it stays that way in the present Bill. As it stands, these huge sums of money will be borrowed without having to come to Parliament for approval and there will be less accountability by the administration for the spending of these funds.
Surely through legislation of this kind we continue to see the erosion of Parliament's control over Crown corporations. Has the Government not learned anything from its past experiences? Has it such a short memory as to forget Canadair, which I believe was in the red to the tune of $1.4 billion, and VIA Rail, which lost $449 million in 1982? 1 understand that VIA Rail forecasts a loss in 1983-84 of some $755 million, de Havilland lost $265.2 million last year. The Post Office has reduced its usual deficit and I believe this past year it was only $300 million, and this with its greatly increased postal rates.
1 recognize and support the fundamental purpose of the Export Development Corporation to assist our manufacturers and small businesses to seek new customers in the international marketplace. On this point, most Hon. Members will agree. The difficulty in the first place, is that there is no requirement that the authorized capital be in the accounts of the corporation; that is, both used and unused authorized capital.
The recent Economic Council report, "Intervention and Efficiency", devotes a full chapter to the subject of export finance and the Export Development Corporation. Government members opposite would do well to read the report, as its thrust is to scale down and reorient the Export Development Corporation and not to enlarge it. Seven of the report's 31 recommendations relate to the Export Development Corporation. One recommendation is that the corporation do less direct financing and that the private sector do more. We could not agree more. The focus of the Economic Council report, as I interpret it, points to a greater say by Parliament in the operations of the corporation. What the amendments propose to do is in the spirit of the report, as the Export Development Corporation presently does not have its spending adequately scrutinized by Parliament. It is not required to table an operating budget or information on the size of its payroll. Moreover, it borrows money in the name of the Canadian taxpayers without seeking parliamentary authority to do so.
The corporation is quite large, with 613 employees. In 1982 it dealt in loan accounts involving 62 exports. It had one customer for every ten employees. As well, it had just over 900 separate insurance policies in 1982 which represented 1.5 policies per employee.
The Government has approximately 306 Crown corporations employing over a quarter of a million people. I believe these corporations have assets totalling close to $75 billion and liabilities of $63 billion. This Bill will increase the borrowing authority of this particular corporation by $35 billion.
I want to assure the House that our Party is dedicated to improving Canada's trade performance and expanding its participation. It is not, however, dedicated to increasing the lack of accountability and control that characterizes the EDC and other Crown corporations.
Indeed, given that there exists the capacity within the existing EDC financing limits, further study hurts no one. As a Crown corporation, EDC should become as commercially viable as possible. As an instrument of public policy, it
September 19, 1983

demands accountability, scrutiny, responsibility and good financial accounting. Would we not be irresponsible if we were to allow for this magnitude of borrowing?
The more the corporation grows, the more it will gobble up tax dollars. The larger the borrowing, the greater the risk. The taxpayers of Canada, particularly in my riding, no longer feel they are getting value for their money and they have good reason. There have been too many instances of Parliament losing control over the constant growth of its size and expenditures.
1 conclude my observations by urging greater responsibility and scrutiny in relation to the present Bill. I believe the amendments are sound and should be adopted. Finally, the Export Development Corporation as a governing policy instrument should not be abused.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak in favour of the amendments proposed by a Member of the Conservative Party of Canada. I do so with a certain sense of knowledge that our nation of Canada in which we have so much faith needs to do more in terms of exports.
I am reminded this morning that in 1968, when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office in this country, Canada exported more goods and services than did the nation of Japan. I stand here some 15 years later with the knowledge that Japan today exports twice as much as Canada. That 15-year period of history is an indictment of the Liberal Party of Canada and the policies which it has put in place in this country as they relate to exports.
Today we are dealing with Bill C-l 10 and two amendments proposed by the Conservative Party of Canada. What is the essence of Bill C-l 10? In its basic thrust, the Liberal Party of Canada, the Cabinet and the Prime Minister are asserting to Canadians that they want to continue in the direction they have been heading and double the amount of money that is flowing to this corporation. The Government has indicated that it does not want to do so with taxpayers' dollars but with borrowed money. It has the mistaken belief that taxpayers' dollars are not at risk by simply turning around and borrowing money.
1 say to the Minister that there are lessons which should be learned from history. I remind him again that this nation exported more than Japan 15 years ago and that Japan now exports twice as much as Canada. Surely the message the Government should learn from that is that we have been on the wrong track as an exporting nation in terms of our policies. Surely we should not have to stand in the House to deal with a Bill which would simply double the amount of money being spent on those policies. Surely 15 years is long enough to make the Government realize that it has been on the wrong track and should not be asking to double the amount of money that it is spending in that direction.
This Bill exemplifies the basic thrust of the Liberal Party's policies over the last 15 years. It represents a denial of the democratic process because it turns power and authority over to appointed bodies with increasing frequency. There are now
Export Development Act
approximately 239,000 Canadians employed by the federal Government who work in Government departments that are accountable to Parliament's elected representatives. Crown corporations, which are removed from the control of Parliament, employ some 262,000 Canadians. More Canadians are employed by Crown corporations than by the federal Government.
As I sat here listening to the interventions of Members of our Party this morning, 1 asked myself what the difference between a democracy and a dictatorship was. There is really very little, if any, difference between the two in a governing sense. Governments of both a dictatorship and a democracy make rules which can take away people's liberty and lives. This is done through criminal laws. As well, these governments pass rules, regulations and laws which take property away from people. The classic example of that is the tax law through which the Government can take a portion of one's goods or money. This is done both in a dictatorship and a democracy.
Therefore, if the powers of a governing dictatorship and democracy are the same, what differentiates a democracy from a dictatorship? The essential difference between the two is simply the ballot box. In a democracy we give a group of people, whether a municipal council, provincial government or federal Parliament, power to take away our lives, liberty or our property in whole or in part. In a democracy these people are elected on a regular basis for perhaps two, three or four years. Those people to whom we give that power are held accountable through universal suffrage, the freedom to vote. That is a very precious principle and I suggest to Liberal backbenchers opposite that it is a very important principle. When people are given the power to remove our liberty or to take away some of our goods or money, we have that vote which holds them accountable. If they do not proceed in a fashion which their electors feel is appropriate or correct, they can throw them out at their next opportunity to vote.
What happens when we give that power to an appointed group, when we give it to a Crown corporation, in this case the Canadian Export Development Corporation? Those appointees are not voted into office, and therefore they cannot be voted out of office. In this piece of legislation before us today we are giving this group of people the same powers that we give to governments, and it is done through the medium of a Crown corporation which is not accountable to Parliament. We are setting up a small, mini-dictatorship. We are transferring powers from Canadian voters to appointed bodies. We are transferring them from a democracy to a dictatorship. That has been the characteristic of the policy of the last 15 years by the present Prime Minister, the present Cabinet as well as preceding Cabinets.
We in the Opposition consistently attempt to enunciate that principle with the greatest clarity possible. We say to the backbenchers opposite: "You have a role and a responsibility. You can participate in the erosion of democracy, you can go into the privacy of your caucus or stand in the public glare of

September 19, 1983
Export Development Act
this chamber and say to the Prime Minister and to the Cabinet that democracy is the most important principle at stake. It must be protected. The good of the nation requires it and you can hold the Cabinet accountable."
Time after time after time we are disappointed because the backbenchers of the Liberal Party will not hold the Cabinet accountable. This supposedly small piece of legislation which sits before us today would empower an unknown group of 15 people to put the taxpayers at risk to the tune of $62,000 million; or to express it another way, to the tune of $62 billion. That amounts to better than two-thirds of total federal spending this year which will be put into the hands of 15 unknown people who cannot be ousted through the ballot box procedure. It is transferring $62,000 million to a dictatorship.
I urge all Members of this chamber to hold this Cabinet accountable and to vote for the amendments proposed by the Conservative Member of Parliament for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to speak today to the amendments to Bill C-110, an Act to amend the Export Development Act.
At the outset I want to make it very, very clear that the Conservative Party is fully committed to increasing foreign trade.
Baloney.

This has always been an integral part of our policy. In fact, the Hon. Member opposite who just said baloney will have to recognize and acknowledge that in 1979 the Conservative Government first made it a provision to have a Member of cabinet fully responsible for foreign trade, and I had the honour to be that first Minister.
It is very clear that the Conservative Party is very much in favour of increasing foreign trade. Increasing foreign trade is the best way possible to increase employment. The way to increase employment is either through domestic or export business. Clearly the increase in domestic business will continue in a normal pattern; sometimes a little faster and sometimes a little slower, but a normal pattern of growth. If we can increase our share of foreign trade by a small percentage in proportion to the over-all export business in the world today, it can have a very large and significant impact on Canada's economy.
Our opposition to this Bill is very clear. It has nothing to do with our position on foreign trade. It does not reflect any weakening in our resolve to increase foreign trade as part of our over-all policy. Our opposition is based on the concern that we have over the accountability of Crown corporations to this Parliament.
It has been very evident over the past few years that this accountability has slipped, and slipped drastically. The Cana-dair example is a text book case of how Crown corporations should not be run. There are some clear strains in the Cana-dair case that apply directly to the Export Development Corporation, and I will be coming to them in a minute, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-110 asks for a blank cheque for the Government and for the Export Development Corporation. It is asking for borrowing authority that could last quite conceivably for the balance of this decade. I want to point out what Professor Andre Raynauld of the University of Montreal said. When referring to the Export Development Corporation, he said it was "rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster". That, I think, says it all. That is something we have to be very aware of and very sensitive to. I hope the Minister is taking account of these observations being made about a corporation under his authority.
The EDC Act normally comes before Parliament about every three or four years. If this Bill goes through in the form proposed, we will probably not see the EDC Act before this Parliament for the next eight or nine years, probably not before 1990. What we are asking for is reasonable control over this Crown corporation. In Motion No. 5 we have asked for a ten to one borrowing ratio on paid-in capital and surplus. Motion No. 3 requests that that authorized capital be limited to $1.1 billion. The current surplus today is close to $200,000. What we have here is an over-all paid-in capital and surplus of $1.3 billion. Ten times that is $13 billion. That means there would be borrowings authorized of $13 billion.
Let us look at what the borrowings are today which total about $4.3 billion. What is the concern? Why are these two amendments, a combination of amendment No. 3 and amendment No. 5, restrictive on the Crown corporation? We have to ask that question and we have not had an answer from the Minister.
We are asking for a borrowing multiplier also on paid-in capital and surplus. The Government has said it wants the multiplier on authorized capital which means capital that is authorized but not necessarily paid into the company. There is quite a significant difference and a very important difference. We have seen how Canadair, as an example, operated on a very low equity basis, borrowed an awful lot of money from banks, from the Government and from international investors, and got into a tremendous amount of trouble, so much so that we had a disaster on our hands and a write-off of $1 billion in taxpayers' money that was invested in Canadair.
If the Government is going to run the Export Development Corporation in the same way as Canadair, we could quite conceivably have another disaster on our hands because there is not that proper check and balance so necessary in running a financial corporation. The Government has not learned the lesson. The Government wants to run this company on fresh air, the same way as it ran Canadair on fresh air. You cannot run a company primarily on borrowings; you have to have that solid equity base. That is why we want to have the borrowing multiplier related to solid equity capital being invested in the company. I am not referring to equity capital in some Minister's mind who says: "Some day we may invest in that company, but not necessarily today". The Minister has not answered that question. He has not stated why the Govern-
September 19, 1983

ment is not prepared to base its borrowing requirement on hard cash which it is prepared to invest directly in the corporation. 1 hope he will respond to that in due course.
The fifth amendment would ensure that the borrowing base is money in the company, not out there in an airy-fairy way in some person's imagination. When I look at the details of our amendment, I realize it is more generous than what 1 originally thought the Bill was allowing. I wondered why we were making an amendment that was more generous. I thought the borrowing multiplier would be based on paid-in capital, and we proposed paid-in capital plus surplus. Then I read it more closely and discovered that it was authorized capital. I look forward to the Minister's explanation on this.
I recognize that there can be some debate on the third amendment. Should the authorized capital be $1.1 billion as we have proposed or $2 billion as the Government has proposed? There is a $900 million difference which represents, with a ten times multiplier, $9 billion of borrowing.
The borrowing of the corporation today which has been built up over its life is approximately $4.5 billion. The difference between what the Government wants to put in and what we want to put in is equal to two times the total amount of borrowings built up over the many years the company has been in existence. That is excessive. It is not responsible and does not demonstrate that the Government is learning its lesson from giving Crown corporations a free hand to run away for three years to ten years before being called to account in Parliament. That is the fundamental issue we are facing today.
I would like to look a little more closely at this area. The growth in borrowings according to the annual report was about $800 million in 1982, the latest year for which we have figures available. That $800 million can be supported by an increase in the capital base of the company of $80 million. The existing authorized capital is $1 billion. That will support borrowings of $10 billion. The borrowings today are $4.5 billion, so there is a tremendous gap between the existing position of the company and where it can go under the current authorized capital, but a tremendous increase over what it wants to do in the next few years.
There has been a lot of pressure put upon us, which I am sure has been instigated by the Minister and his staff, by the exporting community to get the Bill passed because we will reach a crunch where it will not be possible for the EDC to lend any more money to support exports. The Minister has yet to say when that crunch will come. The implication left with us by these people is that it will come in a very few days. I say to the people who are putting this pressure on us that they should show a responsible attitude toward the control of the Export Development Corporation, encourage the Government to show that responsible attitude, and we will show a responsible attitude toward the passage of the Bill. We are reasonable people. We feel that foreign trade should be strongly developed, but we will not roll over or step aside while the Government rapes Parliament and takes taxpayers to the cleaners
Export Development Act
once again with irresponsible action and uncontrolled operations of Crown corporations.

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, lest Elon. Members opposite feel we can move, let me assure them that we will not move until some reason is brought to bear on their apparent unwillingness to move even a little in the direction suggested by the amendments of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). 1 wish more Government backbenchers and indeed some of its frontbenchers, apart from the distinguished three who are here, were present to listen to the arguments being put forth. Then when it comes time to vote on these important matters, they might not simply react to their Whip or Leader, but possibly might find it a useful occasion in which to exercise their best judgment.
I want to deal just briefly with some of the recommendations concerning the question of accountability, which is our fundamental concern and fear. Also 1 would like to deal with the size of the borrowings and the extensions provided in the Bill. They are mind-boggling. In fact, they are more than that; they seriously put into question the capacity of a country the size of Canada to deal with this amount of money. If we look at our weighted borrowings, Government debt, public and private debt for the first 116 years, we realize that the Government is doing more here than government process has done since the mid-1800s. It behooves us to look very closely at it.
The Economic Council of Canada considered these questions in its report on intervention and efficiency. It made a number of recommendations. I will deal with those which pertain to the Export Development Corporation because 1 think they are important. Its recommendations, among others, included the suggestion that the EDC should gradually, not abruptly, move toward providing export credit re-insurance, leaving the field of insurance where it belongs, in the private sector. It further recommended that the EDC serve as the insurer of last resort. Historically it has been attempting to do that, but the Bill before us takes it out of that category and places it in an entirely different position. It is not a lender of last resort, it is not an insurer of last resort. Indeed, Hon. Members over the last several days have indicated that in fact it is becoming a lender of first choice in opposition to the private sector.
Also the report recommended that the EDC continue to provide direct financing for Canadian sales abroad, but only when there is reason to believe that the private sector is unable to provide the required credits. Also it suggested that public financing should be made available only under terms and conditions commensurate with the risks involved, and the cost of such assistance, including the opportunity cost of the funds used, except in cases where it is deemed necessary to take into consideration the export support programs of other countries.
It further recommended that the gradual withdrawal of the EDC from most direct lending activities should be accompanied by an increased concentration of its efforts in the fields of credit insurance and bank guarantees. The corporation

September 19, 1983
should also stand ready to provide refinancing facilities for private lending institutions engaged in export financing. There were eight or ten fundamental recommendations that in fact made sense, all of which pointed to the general problem of Government supplanting that as a policy or principle. Also it recommended that the Government should continue its efforts aUmeetings of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade to obtain an international agreement to limit further subsidized export credit. I will deal with that matter a little later.
May 1 call it one o'clock?

AFTER RECESS

Madam Speaker, nine years have passed since Turkey invaded Cyprus, an independent country and a member of the Commonwealth and the United Nations. The continuing occupation of almost 40 per cent of the territory of Cyprus deprives many Cypriots of their human rights, and hinders the negotiations between the two ethnic communities to work out a formula to live compatibly in peace with each other. The occupation has effectively prevented the United Nations from investigating approximately 1,600 missing persons taken hostage during the days of the invasion, despite repeated resolutions to that effect.
Canada on many occasions in the past has condemned military rule and foreign occupation of sovereign countries, but in the case of Cyprus no such stand has taken place. I respectfully request that our Government demonstrate a more just and courageous position toward Cyprus by voting in favour of all resolutions in the United Nations aimed at condemnation of the continuing occupation of Cyprus, and seeking to resolve the human tragedy of missing persons. Unless the Cyprus problem is resolved according to the principles of self-determination of sovereign nations, the cause of democracy, freedom of all nations, and human rights for all people of the world, will not be sincerely served.

Madam Speaker, since 1959 the Farm Credit Corporation has been a valuable tool for farmers in their quest for funding. However, the demand now for Farm Credit Corporation funds grows faster than the Corporation's budget. The Farm Credit Corporation recently asked the Government's permission to borrow $600 million on the financial market, but was allowed to borrow only $250 million. The amount is already spoken for. This action by the Government confirms that it does not understand the importance and need for Farm Credit Corporation money in agriculture.
If the Government is truly concerned about jobs it had better look at the agricultural industry, an area where its action, or lack of it, is causing unprecedented bankruptcies and unemployment. In the short term, the Farm Credit Corporation should be allowed to borrow all the funds it needs. In the long term, an agribond system must be introduced, that is, if the Government is concerned about saving agriculture.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-REFUGEE DENIED PERMISSION TO ATTEND PARENT'S FUNERAL

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: U.S.S.R.-REFUGEE DENIED PERMISSION TO ATTEND PARENT'S FUNERAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, approximately seven years ago Lilia Karp and her husband, Lev Karp, were allowed to leave the Soviet Union, but only after considerable pressure had been exerted by President Ford, Secretary of State Kissinger, and Senator Hubert Humphrey of the United States. The difficulty Mr. Karp had found himself in was that, in his home in Moscow, he had endeavoured to teach Soviet technocrats a number of the new western technologies. By leaving Russia he was able to escape the pressure of the KGB. He and his wife are now living in North York with their two children.
On August 22 the mother of Lilia Karp died in Moscow. Upon learning of her mother's death Mrs. Karp sought to go to Moscow but was unable to obtain Soviet permission. Last Saturday morning Lilia Karp learned of the death of her father who, according to her, died of a broken heart because he was unable to have his daughter with him at the funeral of the mother. The funeral of the father is going to be held next Saturday.
I urge members of the Soviet Embassy here to work with the Karps to ensure that Lilia Karp can be in Moscow for her parents funeral. This is not a time for politics. This is a time for humanity.
September 19, 1983

Madam Speaker, on the last sitting day one of my colleagues in the House of Commons complained about the aesthetic damage caused by the Peace Camp on the lawns of Parliament Hill. Probably many people agreed with that. However, I would like to say that if an atomic weapon of the size of the Cruise missile, which can carry a 200-kilaton bomb, which is equal to 200,000 tons of TNT, which is equal to 400 boxcar loads of high explosive, fell on the lawn of Parliament Hill, this building and all the buildings around here would be vaporized. Everybody in this building would likewise disappear.
We would be the fortunate ones because, within the one kilometre to 1.5 kilometre range in Ottawa, all buildings would be pulverized, destroyed, and left in ruin. Within three kilometres, 90 per cent of all people would die. That would include all of downtown Ottawa, as far away as the Governor General's home, and would include Hull and Vanier.
A firestorm would take over for 80 square kilometres and suffocation from heat, and a lack of oxygen would leave the people in Gatineau, Kanata and Old Chelsea dying or dead. A firestorm would start the forests of the Gatineau Hills on fire. Finally, there would be a crater 600 metres across and 75 metres deep where the House of Commons now stands. The demonstration is a bit messy, but what the people there are trying to say is, "stop in the name of humanity".

speechtext: The Hon. Member's time is up.

Madam Speaker, I want to express my pleasure at the recent signing of the U.S.-Canada agreement to track long-range pollution, the Captex project. I note that this is the first act of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia), and 1 hope that this will be far from his last.
In looking more closely at this experiment, however, I wonder about its real significance. Do we not already know that acid rain comes from the valleys of Ohio? What about the Minister's caution against attaching undue significance to the experiment? What does that mean? Has he that little confidence?
1 trust that the Minister will be more optimistic, forceful, and more representative in bringing this vital issue to the attention of his cabinet colleagues. That means more money so that we may have a higher profile and the issue will have the true representation it deserves. In other words, we must put our money where our mouth is.

maintopic: S O. 21 INDUSTRY WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD -THREAT TO DEALER NETWORK
S O. 21 INDUSTRY WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD -THREAT TO DEALER NETWORK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the jobs of 1,000 employees, and the future of 125 White Farm Equipment Ltd. dealerships across Canada and their employees, will be in jeopardy if the Government of Canada does not take action to ensure that the company continue in operation. It is understood that the Government has refused to consider the offer of the U.S. division of the company which submitted the highest bid, and favours the sale of the technology for the axial flow combine to Massey-Ferguson. Such a move could result in the dissolution of the White Farm Equipment dealer network in Canada with consequent bankruptcies and/or substantial financial loss, and the elimination of hundreds of jobs for those employed by the dealers.
In addition, well over 100,000 farmers across Canada who own White equipment would be unable to take action on the guarantees covering their equipment, would be unable or find it difficult to obtain repairs and at the same time be faced with the situation where their equipment will have little if any trade-in value. This matter is urgent and requires immediate action on the part of the Government to negotiate an arrangement to ensure the continued operation of the company.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-PLIGHT OF LEV AND INA ELBERT ARRESTED BY KGB
U.S.S.R.-PLIGHT OF LEV AND INA ELBERT ARRESTED BY KGB
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to raise with the House of Commons a problem which confronts Lev and Ina Elbert, in Kiev in the Ukraine. You will recall when we were in Moscow I raised with Soviet officials the problem of Lev Elbert, in as much as he had been improperly arrested and jailed simply because he wanted to leave the Soviet Union. I raised that question with them as a result of his wife having come all the way from Kiev to meet with me in Moscow.
When she arrived back in Kiev, she was arrested after KGB agents walked in and picked a book off the bookshelf, opened it, and found some substance which they claimed to be drugs. Her husband is now under detention. He has done no wrong except to ask that he be granted the privileges and rights that are afforded each world citizen under the Helsinki Accord. She is on a hunger strike. She is going to die unless some action is taken to try to right this terrible wrong. I ask each and every Member of Parliament to write today to the Supreme Soviet, asking them to look into this matter and find some reasonable humane solution.

September 19, 1983

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO IMPORTATION OF RUSSIAN-BUILT LADA CARS
OPPOSITION TO IMPORTATION OF RUSSIAN-BUILT LADA CARS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on November 16, 1982, I moved a motion under Standing Order 43 urging the Canadian Government to take all necessary steps to protect Canadian workers from the unfair competition of the Russian-made automobile, Lada, because many of its parts are made in prison camps and it is manufactured by non-union workers.
A few days later I received a telephone call from someone who would not give his name and who spoke broken English, who wanted me to rescind the motion, and I told him that I had no intention of so doing. He was quite angry and advised me that it would be much better if I did not move any further motions of that kind. I advised him that I intended to continue to deplore and publicize the slave labour of the communists, not only in manufacturing Lada, but also for invading Afghanistan, imprisoning Walesa in Poland, et cetera. He banged down the receiver. Premier Davis of Ontario has now asked Ontarians not to buy Soviet made Lada cars because of the shooting down of the Korean passenger plane, which again indicates the low value the communists place on human lives.
I urge the Canadian Government to prevent the importation of Lada cars or, at the very least, impose a tax or duty that would make their retail price competitive with the vehicles manufactured in countries where the workers receive a living wage for their work.
Why should Canadians help the Soviet communists who would, at the drop of a hat, invade northern Canada just as they invaded Afghanistan-if they determined that we could not defend ourselves?

subtopic: LEGALITY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUDGET LEGISLATION
LEGALITY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUDGET LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on July 26, this year I wrote to the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) about the British Columbia budget legislation as being an assault on human rights and fundamental justice. I said that in my opinion parts of it could violate the due process clause of the Canadian Charter of Rights. I have a reply from the Minister dated September 13. The Minister refuses to state an opinion as to the legality of the legislation. In my letter I had asked that he give aid, through the Department of Justice, to litigants who want to challenge the legislation in court. The Minister refused to do that as well, saying that the court program is restricted to language cases. It seems to me, Madam Speaker, that this is in conflict with what the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) said this summer, and it also makes it very hard for the little guy to fight the legislation in the courts.
I urge the Government to do more than simply monitor the British Columbia legislation because as an assault on human rights in Canada, it could be a foretaste of things to come. I urge it also to give aid to people who would like to launch a case to test the constitutionality of that legislation.

subtopic: DEMAND FOR PUBLIC INVESTIGATION OF ACCIDENT ATGIMLI, MANITOBA
DEMAND FOR PUBLIC INVESTIGATION OF ACCIDENT ATGIMLI, MANITOBA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there seems to be an urgent need for a public inquiry into the crash landing of an Air Canada Boeing 767 at Gimli, Manitoba, this past summer, because this aircraft is reported to have taken off with insufficient fuel to reach its scheduled place of landing, with some 69 people aboard.
In the United States there is a tradition of holding public inquiries over safety matters in air travel. In contrast, in Canada there is a "behind closed doors" approach, with that information only becoming public if the president of Air Canada wishes. It should be noted that Members of Parliament will be denied access to the evidence given at the Gimli investigation.
As a matter of public safety in air travel, the Government owes Canadians an open public investigation, with the press in attendance. For an Air Canada jet to be allowed to take off with insufficient fuel is a serious matter in the minds of Canadians. If the Government sits idly by and watches the seven-man commission study this incident behind closed doors, with five of the committee being paid employees of the Boeing company, it will be guilty of a dereliction of its responsibility to the Canadian public. It would be like asking five engineers of the General Motors Corporation if the car they designed is safe. The public of Canada will not accept this Air Canada coverup.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. For months the Minister has been sitting on the problem related to White Farm Equipment. To date, there does not seem to be any resolution of the problem other than the fact that an order appears to be imminent, or has already been given, for the liquidation of the company. This will result in the loss of dealers and the loss of Canadian White equipment

line, leading to the loss of many jobs. What has the Minister done to date to avoid this disaster?

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE REPORT-RECOMMENDATION ON CANADIAN CONTENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Government has had in its hands for over four months a task force report on the automotive industry in Canada, which outlines how we could get an additional 35,000 jobs on a fairness principle, if the Government cared to act. SITUATION VIS-A-VIS AMERICAN, JAPANESE AND GERMAN COMPANIES

for Toyota, Datsun and Volkswagen? Why is the Minister not making that recommendation to his Cabinet colleagues?

subsubtopic: EXCLUSION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY FROM PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question, which is directed to the Minister of Transport, relates to his Crow legislation. As he knows, the Crow Bill which is before Parliament specifically excludes, from the receipt of any benefits the British Columbia Railway, which, in turn, would deprive farmers in the Peace River country of British Columbia from receiving any benefits in getting their grain to market. Indeed, it would deprive farmers in the Peace River region of Alberta from using the interchange with the BCR to get their grain to the closest point on the West Coast.
Notwithstanding the deliberations and discussions of the committee on the Crow Bill, has the Minister undertaken thus far to speak with the Government of British Columbia, specifically, and with the railway, as to the kind of arrangement that can be made to embrace the British Columbia Railway in the national system; in other words, to remove from it the stigma which it now has of being a foreign railway?

subsubtopic: EXCLUSION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY FROM PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me first say that never will I stand aside the functioning of any committee of this Commons. I think it is very important to ensure that the Commons committee, which travelled across the country and heard a wide variety of representations, be heard and that we carefully listen to its proposals and advice. So, unlike the Hon. Member, 1 do not put it aside. In fact, in front of the committee I clearly indicated that I would be both willing to listen to its views on the issue, and responsive, as to how we might proceed. I look forward to the recommendations or amendments that the committee would like to put forth.
As far as the British Columbia Railway being a foreign railway is concerned, that is not the case. However, the British Columbia Railway does not recognize the jurisdiction of the federal Government in transportation, particularly the obligation to be under the regulatory jurisdiction of the Canadian Transport Commission. If the BCR wanted to undertake that kind of commitment it would then be much easier for the Government of Canada to reciprocate and therefore deal with
it in a way similar to other railways. Therefore, if the Hon. Member wants to indicate to the British Columbia Railway its responsibility, then he can be assured that we are certainly willing to undertake those kinds of discussions.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. As he may know, Air Canada itself has commissioned a group of experts to look into its safety procedures. As a major shareholder of Air Canada, 1 expect to have that report in my possession within a matter of days and that the results of that report and whatever corrections it will request would be immediately undertaken by Air Canada. I would also like to report to the House that I have asked the departmental officials to undertake a major audit of the operating activities of Air Canada. That will commence at the end of this month, and we will have a full report. That would obviously be a matter of public disclosure at that time.
I would like to take this opportunity to say that when it comes to the issue of examining and having public inquiries on air safety matters, there is a bill to establish a new air safety

board presently before the Transport committee. If the Opposition were to co-operate we could get that legislation through very quickly and into the House so that we could have a proper mechanism under which public inquiries could be undertaken.
